node.name: Daily Worship at Marquand Chapel
node.descriptionText:
Join us at 11:30am in Marquand Chapel for our daily worship.

Worship in Marquand often draws on a wide variety of inherited Christian traditions, with the worship of many denominations being represented. Beyond that, though, we also pay attention to the rising number of people in Western society who have a lively interest in spirituality but feel no connection to traditional forms of church and worship. So Marquand is also actively engaged in original, creative, and experimental forms of worship, both for committed Christians and for those exploring the faith.

node.name: Scaling Biochar Solutions: From Field Observations to Global Modeling - CIE Lunchtime Series
node.descriptionText:
Can biochar deliver consistent climate and agricultural benefits from individual fields to the global scale? Biochar, a carbon-rich material derived from biomass, has the potential to improve soil health, enhance agricultural productivity, and mitigate climate change. However, its effectiveness varies considerably across environmental conditions and management practices, raising questions about its long-term and large-scale impacts. In this seminar, Professor Wei Ren will present her team's research that integrates field observations, global data synthesis, and process-based ecosystem modeling to examine how biochar affects soil carbon storage, nutrient cycling, greenhouse gas emissions, and crop productivity. Together, these approaches help explain the environmental controls and underlying mechanisms shaping biochar responses across locations and over time, while identifying uncertainties in its long-term effectiveness. The seminar will also provide a basis for discussing how these findings can inform broader assessments of biochar deployment and carbon removal, with potential connections to industrial ecology and the bioeconomy.

Dr. Wei Ren is an Associate Professor in the Department of Natural Resources and the Environment at the University of Connecticut. Her research focuses on understanding the interactions among climate change, human activities, and terrestrial ecosystems, with particular emphasis on carbon and nutrient cycling, ecosystem sustainability, and climate-smart agriculture. Her interdisciplinary research integrates field observations, remote sensing, global data synthesis, machine learning, and process-based ecosystem modeling to investigate ecosystem responses to environmental change and evaluate the effectiveness of sustainable land management practices across spatial and temporal scales. Her work aims to advance predictive understanding of ecosystem dynamics and inform science-based strategies for climate change mitigation and adaptation, sustainable agriculture, and natural resource management.

node.name: Interwoven: Sounds and Visions from the World’s Refugee Camps
node.descriptionText:
This retrospective exhibition of community art and traditional music will be on view at the Yale Institute of Sacred Music’s Miller Hall at 406 Prospect Street, New Haven from October 15 -December 3 on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays from 12 - 4 p.m., except for Thanksgiving week when the ISM is closed.

Presented by Artolution, an international community-based public arts, education, and mental health organization that uses creative expression to build connection, resilience, and community, the exhibition is organized by Dr. Max Frieder, Artolution Co-Founder and Chief Creative Officer (read more about Dr. Frieder below).

Building on the acclaimed exhibition Interwoven: Exchange Artworks Made Between Refugee Camps Around the World, originally launched at the United Nations, this expanded presentation hosted at the ISM brings together large-scale collaborative artworks, video documentation of traditional folkloric musicians, and cultural artifacts created by displaced communities across five continents.

The exhibition creates a dialogue between visual art and music in contexts of displacement and crisis. Alongside the artworks, visitors encounter videos of musicians from the same communities, offering an opportunity to experience not only the remarkable stories behind the works, but also the sounds, movements, languages, rhythms, and creative traditions of the people who made them.

Together, these works offer a powerful portrait of communities using art, music, and cultural expression to preserve identity, share their stories, and create connections across borders.

node.name: Human Rights Workshop:  Violeta Canaves, "Is a Global Reproductive Justice Movement Still Possible? Reflections on Global Inequalities and Human Rights Advocacy"
node.descriptionText:
Lunch Provided / RSVP Required. Email the Schell Center at schell.law@yale.edu to request background readings a week prior to talk.

Violeta Canaves serves as the Senior Advocacy Advisor at the International Planned Parenthood Federation in New York, where she supports and advises states in United Nations negotiations on sexual and reproductive health and rights and gender equality, and plays a leading role in a global civil society coalition advancing reproductive justice at the U.N.. Her work focuses on using human rights law as a tool for systemic change, in close collaboration with both state actors and social movements. For over a decade, Violeta served as a Professor of Constitutional Law and Human Rights at the Universidad Nacional del Litoral in Argentina, while also being actively engaged in Argentina’s National Campaign for the Right to Free, Legal, and Safe Abortion. She brings a rare combination of grassroots movement experience in Argentina and technical leadership within global institutions, including roles with UNFPA and the International Planned Parenthood Federation.  Violeta holds an LL.M. and a JSD from Yale Law School, and her first law degree from the Universidad Nacional del Litoral in Argentina.

node.name: Public power for planetary health equity: why ownership matters
node.descriptionText:
Due to industrial action at University of Technology Sydney (where guest speaker, Matt Ryan, works) on 30th April, the webinar has been postponed to November.

As we overshoot our climate targets, the solution remains crystal clear: stop burning fossil fuels, and build more renewables – but who should build them, and why? The norm in places with privatised energy systems (like Australia) is for these new infrastructures to be privately owned, developed to generate ongoing profits. In this webinar, drawing on perspectives from history and political economy, Matt will explore the case for publicly owned renewable power. It would seem that this approach is preferable across the grounds of emissions reduction, equity, engineering, and cost – so what is the catch? As we increasingly question privatisation across many aspects of economic life, it is time to revisit power.

The ‘Saving the World’ webinar series, presented by the Planetary Health Equity Hothouse, releases a new episode each month, discussing the intersections between climate change, inequity and human health. The webinars focus on actions that enable transformative change away from the harmful consumptogenic system to systems that promote good health, social equity and environmental wellbeing.

Please do not join our webinars with an AI notetaker. If this is essential for you, for accessibility reasons, please email us prior to the webinar.

Teaching Languages at the Yale University Art Gallery 
Join Candace Skorupa, Senior Lector I, French, and Lecturer, Comparative Literature, and Yale University Art Gallery educators to explore strategies for effectively incorporating engagement with works of art into your language courses.  
The Yale University Art Gallery offers a rich educational environment for teaching world languages and cultures and expanding students’ horizons. This interactive workshop draws upon many of the excellent tips and ideas in the newly published resource, A Practical Guide to Teaching Languages at the Yale University Art Gallery (attached). Whether you’re new to teaching in the museum or a seasoned pro, we invite you to come together with fellow language instructors to explore new ideas, ask questions, and share your successes and challenges with the group.  

Note: This interactive workshop will take place in the galleries at the Yale University Art Gallery, 1111 Chapel Street. Please plan to eat your lunch before or after the workshop, as we will not have food or drink in the museum during the session.

Registration required. Up to 35 participants.

node.name: Yale NSG Coffee with Mike Fuchs
node.descriptionText:
Come for an informal coffee with Mike Fuchs, with Atticus coffee and pastries. 

Michael H. Fuchs is currently the U.S. Foreign Policy program director at the Open Society Foundations. He joined OSF after leaving his role as at the White House as the Deputy Chief of Staff for Vice President Kamala Harris from 2021-2022. 

He was previously a Senior Fellow at American Progress, where his work focuses on U.S. foreign policy priorities and U.S. policy toward the Asia-Pacific. Fuchs also serves as a senior policy advisor at J Street.

From 2013 to 2016, Fuchs served as deputy assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, directing U.S. policy on the South China Sea, regional security issues, and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN, and managing the bureau’s foreign assistance budget of almost $800 million.

Fuchs was special advisor to the secretary of state for strategic dialogues from 2011 to 2013, leading planning and preparation for Secretary of State Hillary Clinton’s strategic dialogues with China, India, South Africa, and others. During this time, Fuchs also served as a member of the secretary’s policy planning staff, where he worked on a diverse set of issues and initiatives including the department’s response to the Arab Spring, cybersecurity, and the development of a U.S. government strategy to prevent and respond to mass atrocities. From 2009 to 2011, Fuchs was special assistant to Secretary Clinton, providing day-to-day and long-term policy advice on the full range of U.S. foreign policy issues.

Before joining the U.S. State Department, Fuchs served as deputy national security director for Hillary Clinton’s 2008 presidential campaign, where he helped run policy, outreach, and communications on all foreign policy and defense issues for the campaign.

Previously, Fuchs worked on foreign policy and energy and environment issues for American Progress, co-directed a project on democracy and U.S. foreign policy for The Century Foundation, and ran a human rights project in Afghanistan. He has also been a lecturer at George Washington University, where he taught courses on politics and policymaking.

Fuchs co-authored The Survival and the Success of Liberty: A Democracy Agenda for U.S. Foreign Policy with Morton H. Halperin. He is a graduate of Columbia University and a term member of the Council on Foreign Relations.

node.name: Big Brothers Big Sisters
node.descriptionText:
Big Brothers Big Sisters requires a unique application process to be fully prepared to work with New Haven Public School Students. Please read below!


Since 1904, Big Brothers Big Sisters (BBBS) has helped children realize their potential and build their futures through meaningful mentorship. BBBS Connecticut and Dwight Hall are partnering to provide mentorship to the children at Truman School in New Haven.

We are seeking caring Yale students to become "Bigs" - mentors who support the dreams of, listen to, and empower students at Truman School. By becoming a "Big", you will join a tight-knit community that fosters education and collaboration, develop friendships with other mentors, and most importantly, create a lifelong bond with a Truman School student.

Please note that this position requires a weekly commitment on Thursdays from 2:30-5pm (3-4:30pm without transportation time) for the 2024-25 academic year. Transportation will be provided by the program. Limited spots are available and decisions are made on a rolling basis.

Below is the process of applying to this position:
Complete the BBBS application here: BBBS Application.
Once you have submitted this application, submit the Yale Connect form: https://cglink.me/2dA/s95475
We will then review your application. Once it is approved, you will be able to register for this opportunity under the "Service Opportunities" page in Yale Connect, which can be found here: Service Opportunities.
Approving applications typically takes one week. If you have any questions, please email j.navarro@yale.edu. We look forward to reading your applications!

node.name: Lost in New Haven: Museum Tour & Happy Hour with OISS
node.descriptionText:
A collab between OISS and Sustainability Office to show you the basics of vermicomposting, all participants get a worm bin with live worms.

Are you an international student or scholar interested in composting but don't have an outdoor space to put it into practice? Sounds like you could use some help setting up your own indoor worm composting (vermicomposting) system!

Vermicomposting is an environmentally friendly and accessible way to turn everyday organic waste (such as coffee grounds, eggshells, and fruit peels) into nutrient-rich compost, also known as worm castings. You can then use the compost for your potted plants or in a community garden.



During the program, you will learn about:

The basics and science of vermicomposting, with a live demonstration
How to start your own worm bin, with all supplies provided
Yale and New Haven resources for composting and recycling


Your registration fee includes:

A fully set-up, portable worm bin with live worms, bedding, and other essential supplies (we will build the worm bin together during the session)
Light refreshments


Notes Before You Book & Ticket Pricing

Open to international students and scholars
This workshop involves live worms. Please handle them gently and respectfully, and be mindful of their well-being throughout their lifecycle.
All ticket sales are final. No refunds will be issued.
Questions? Contact International Community Engagement Specialist Charlie Lee at charlie.lee@yale.edu.

Join OISS for an evening in Wooster Square as we explore one of New Haven’s newest gems, the Lost in New Haven museum!

Join OISS for an evening in Wooster Square as we explore one of New Haven’s newest gems, the Lost in New Haven museum! This beautifully curated space tells the story of New Haven from past to present.

We’ll begin with a guided tour led by Rob Greenberg, founder of Lost in New Haven, who will share an inside look at how he curated this remarkable collection to tell the story of our city.

What makes this museum especially unique? It has a fully functional bar! Your ticket includes museum admission and one drink during Lost in New Haven’s happy hour, which we’ll enjoy together after the tour.

Located in a converted warehouse on Hamilton Street, Lost in New Haven blends a museum and cultural hub into one immersive space. With artful design, a top-notch sound system, a historic bar, and compelling exhibits, it is the Elm City’s social parlor, welcoming neighbors and tourists alike to celebrate the breadth and vibrancy of New Haven, Connecticut.
